Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).
Motivation
System tests are the only tests that run Kafka as real processes, yet contributors run them
least: writing one means learning Python and ducktape, and running one locally means setting up
ducker nodes. So few people write them, and their failures surface late, in nightly runs.
This KIP makes system tests as easy to write and run as integration tests: same language, same
JUnit framework,@ClusterTest-style annotations, with containers as the execution mode. That
also means less to maintain, and some tests get much faster (the compression test went from ~85s
to ~12s).
It also lets tests use Kafka the way users do. Command line tools can drive real operations, so
gaps between them and the Admin API are caught: while implementing
[KIP-1066](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/311627566/KIP-1066+Mechanism+to+cordon+brokers+and+log+directories),
a scenario worked through the Admin API but not throughkafka-configs.sh, and only manual
testing found it.
The trade-off is version coverage: the suite supports Kafka 4.0 and later, because it runs KRaft
only and ZooKeeper mode was removed in 4.0. Tests that need older releases, such as compatibility
with 2.x clients, stay in ducktape.
Proposed Changes
A newsystemtestsmodule with JUnit 5 tests that run Kafka in containers (Testcontainers),
started from Kafka's official Docker image. It needs only Docker or Podman, so it can run on a
laptop, and it has its own Gradle task, separate from./gradlew test.
@ClusterSystemTest
Tests declare their cluster with @ClusterSystemTest, which looks like @ClusterTestand uses
the same JUnit extension. It is a separate annotation because some of @ClusterTest's attributes
cannot apply to a container cluster, such as metadataVersion,which the image decides, and a few options,
such as the images to run, apply only to containers.@ClusterSystemTest(types = {Type.KRAFT, Type.CO_KRAFT}, brokers = 3, controllers = 3,
brokerSecurityProtocol = SecurityProtocol.SASL_SSL,
serverProperties =@ClusterConfigProperty(key = "sasl.enabled.mechanisms", value = "SCRAM-SHA-512"),
parameters =@ClusterParameter(name = "failureMode", values = {"clean_bounce", "hard_bounce"}))
voidtestReplication(ClusterInstance cluster,@Param("failureMode") FailureMode failureMode) { ... }
Each combination runs as its own invocation on a fresh cluster. The runtime provisions
what the configuration implies,such as TLS certificates, SASL users and a Kerberos KDC,
so tests do not set these up themselves. Other options can cover, for example, cross-version
runs over several images, dynamic KRaft quorums, several log directories per broker, tiered
storage and network faults.
Containers for clients, Connect and Streams
The test's own Admin client, producer and consumer connect from the test JVM. Everything else that
talks to the cluster runs in its own container on the cluster's network, the way users run it: the shipped
verifiable and console clients, standalone and distributed Connect workers, and Streams applications
from the Streams test jar. A client or Streams container can use a different image than the brokers,
which is what cross-version tests need.
Faults, restarts and upgrades
Each node is a real process in its own container, with its own data volume, so tests can exercise
what a real deployment goes through, for example:
Clean stops and hard kills (SIGTERM and SIGKILL).
Network partitions, latency and bandwidth limits.
Log directory failures.
Nodes that lose their data, or join after the cluster has started.
Rolling restarts with changed configuration, listeners or security protocols.
Rolling upgrades to another release over the same data.
Command line tools
The plan is to cover the shipped CLIs by running them in a container against the cluster, so
operations are tested
